en: The Therāpadāna,
Buddhavagga 3.
The Apadāna of the Elder Sāriputta
Now, listen to the legend of the Elder:
"Not far from the Himalayas,
there is a mountain named Lambaka."
My hermitage is well-constructed,
my leaf-hut is beautifully arranged;
the river has its banks made easy to ford.
Well-situated and delightful,
strewn with very pure sand,
it is not far from my hermitage.
There a river flows, free from gravel and without precipices, sweet and without a foul odor.
Adorning my hermitage:
there are crocodiles, sea-monsters, and here too, sharks and turtles.
There they move about in the river,
beautifying my hermitage:
the pāṭhīna fish and the pāvusa fish.
The *balaja*, *muñja*, and *rohitaka* grasses, and the *vaggaḷa* reeds as they rustle,
beautify my hermitage.
On both banks of the river,
trees are flowering and bearing fruit,
hanging down on both sides.
They beautify my hermitage:
the mango, the sal, the tilaka,
the trumpet-flower, and the sinduvāraka.
Celestial fragrances waft about,
as the campaka, saḷala, and nīpa trees have blossomed in my hermitage.
Nāgas, punnāgas, and ketakas,
having blossomed in my hermitage, waft forth divine fragrances.
Atimuttā and Asoka,
and the Bhaginīmālā in full bloom;
Aṅkola and Bimbijālā, too.
In my hermitage,
the ketakā, kandali, godhuka,
and tiṇasūlika trees are all in bloom.
Exuding a divine fragrance,
they beautify my hermitage—
the kaṇikāra and kaṇṇikā trees.
Many *asanā* and *ajjunā* trees,
wafting divine fragrances,
beautify my hermitage.
Punnāga trees, mountain punnāgas,
and koviḷāra trees are in bloom,
wafting a divine fragrance.
They beautify my hermitage:
uddālaka trees, kuṭajas,
kadambas, and many bakulas.
Exuding a divine fragrance,
they beautify my hermitage—
alaka grass and mung beans.
The plantains and citron trees,
nurtured with scented water,
bear their fruit.
Some lotuses are blooming,
others are being born with filaments;
some lotuses have already flowered.
Then, in the pond, the lotuses were in bloom; they conceived fruit,
and their stalks and fibers spread forth.
Strewn with *siṅghāṭika* flowers,
the ponds then shine;
they are fragrant with the scent of mangoes and are carried along.
Uttalī and bandhujīvaka flowers,
possessing divine fragrance,
were then in full bloom upon the pond.
The pāṭhīna, the pāvusa fish,
the balaja, the muñja, and the rohita;
the saṅgula and the maggura as well.
Then they dwell in the pond:
crocodiles, sharks, and rakshasas that seize with their cords.
Owls and pythons dwelt there at that time in the lake,
as did pigeons and sun-swans.
Cakravāka birds that frequent the river,
cuckoos, parrots, and sāḷikas—
all depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
The kukkutthakas, the kuḷīrakas,
the pokkharasātakas in the forest,
the dindibhas, and the suvapotas—
Swans, cranes, and peacocks, cuckoos and *tambacūḷaka* birds, all depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
The pammakas and the jīvañjīvas depend upon that lake;
so too do the kosikas and the poṭṭhasīsas.
Many ospreys and senaka birds,
as well as mahākāla birds,
depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
Pasadas, boars,
yaks, and many gaṇḍakas;
rohiccas and white pigeons.
Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, and jackals depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
The mātaṅga elephants, divided into three herds,
depend upon that lake;
as do the kinnaras and the monkeys.
Furthermore, forest workers,
hunters, and fowlers all depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
The tinduka, the piyāla,
the madhuka, and the kāsumārī trees surely bear their fruits.
Not far from my hermitage are the *kosaṃba*,
*saḷala*, and *nimba* trees,
endowed with sweet fruit.
Surely they bear fruit not far from my hermitage—
the harītaka and the āmalaka.
The mango, the rose-apple,
and the vibhītaka; the kola, the bhallātaka,
and the billa— these bear fruits.
Āluvā and kaḷambā,
biḷālī and takkaḷa;
jīvaka and sutaka as well.
Many are my hermitages.
Not far from the hermitage,
there are well-constructed ponds.
With clear water and cool currents,
with beautiful landing-stairs, and enchanting;
covered with lotuses and water-lilies.
It is filled with white lotuses,
covered with mandārava flowers,
and a divine fragrance wafts forth.
Thus, in this forest endowed with every excellence,
in full bloom and bearing fruit,
in a well-constructed and delightful hermitage—
I was dwelling at that time,
virtuous and perfected in vows,
a meditator always delighting in jhāna.
The ascetic named Suruci, who had attained the power of the five higher knowledges,
[had] twenty-four thousand...
These disciples attended upon me;
all of them were brahmins,
of noble birth and renowned for their glory.
In the science of marks, in history,
and in the Nighaṇṭu and Keṭubha lexicons;
in the analysis of words and in grammar—
They have reached perfection in the true Dhamma;
they are skilled in portents, omens, and bodily marks.
On the earth, on the ground, and in the sky,
my well-trained disciples—
these few in desire and prudent ones— [move].
Taking little food and free from greed,
content with gain and loss,
they always attend upon me.
The wise ones who meditate, delighting in jhāna,
with peaceful minds and concentrated,
aspire to the state of nothingness.
They always attend upon me—
those who have reached perfection in direct knowledge and delight in the ancestral domain.
Wise beings who roam through the air always surround me;
they are well-restrained at the six sense-doors.
Unshaken, with guarded faculties,
and unattached— those wise ones,
my disciples, are difficult to overcome.
Sitting cross-legged,
by means of standing and walking meditation,
they pass the night.
My disciples are difficult to assail:
they do not become attached to what is attractive,
nor do they feel aversion toward what is repulsive.
My disciples, difficult to approach, are not deluded by that which causes delusion;
they investigate psychic power.
They move about at all times;
through their insolence, those who are difficult to approach cause the earth to tremble.
And those disciples,
while playing, play the game of jhāna;
they bring back fruits from the rose-apple tree.
My disciples are difficult to assail.
Some go to Goyāna,
others to Pubbavideha.
And others, difficult to approach, sent a basket ahead from Uttarakuru for the sake of seeking [food].
And they follow behind him;
with twenty-four thousand [beings],
the sky is covered.
Some cook with fire, some without fire;
some use their teeth as a mortar,
while others grind with a stone.
They subsisted on fallen fruit;
some practiced descending into water,
and others remained pure and steadfast morning and evening.
My disciples, difficult to approach, perform the ritual sprinkling with water;
their armpits, nails, and body hair are grown long.
With mud-stained teeth and dust upon their heads,
my disciples are difficult to overcome, being perfumed with the fragrance of virtue.
Having assembled early in the morning,
those matted-hair ascetics of fierce austerities proclaimed their gains and losses.
Then they travel through the sky.
As these beings depart,
a great sound arises.
At the sound of the deer-skin robe,
the deities rejoice and depart in every direction.
The seers who roam through the sky,
supported by their own power,
go wherever they wish.
These are all sky-goers who cause the earth to tremble; possessed of fierce energy,
they are difficult to overcome.
Unshakable like the ocean:
some sages were standing or walking,
while others remained seated.
Some of my disciples, who subsist on alms-food, are difficult to approach;
they dwell in loving-kindness.
They seek the welfare of all living beings;
not praising themselves,
they do not disparage anyone at all.
Fearless like a lion king,
powerful like a lordly elephant,
and difficult to approach like a tiger.
They come into my presence:
the *vidyādharas*, the deities,
the *nāgas*, the *gandharvas*, and the *rākṣasas*.
Kumbhaṇḍas, dānavas, and garuḷas depend upon that lake;
they are laden with matted hair and baskets.
Clad in upper garments of antelope skin,
all those who roam the sky depend upon that lake for their livelihood.
These twenty-four thousand [monks] are always appropriate [to one another], respectful toward each other.
No sound of throwing down is heard.
Placing foot upon foot,
making little noise and well-restrained;
Having approached,
they all paid homage to me with their heads.
Surrounded by those disciples, I—
And with peaceful ascetics;
there I dwelt in that hermitage,
a meditator devoted to meditation.
By the fragrance of the virtue of the seers,
by the fragrance of flowers, and by the fragrance of the fruit of those who bear fruit— both together.
The hermitage is fragrant.
I do not distinguish between night and day;
no discontent exists within me.
When I advise my own children,
I find even greater joy than when seeing flowers in full bloom.
And as the fruits ripen,
divine fragrances waft forth,
beautifying my hermitage.
Having emerged from concentration,
ardent and discerning,
I took up a load of a khāri.
I plunged into the forest.
I was well-trained in portents, dreams, and the science of bodily marks.
I then retained the mantra words as they were being recited.
The Blessed One Anomadassī—
The eldest in the world, the bull among men,
the perfectly awakened one who desires solitude,
approached the Himalayas.
Having plunged into the Himalayas,
the supreme, compassionate Sage sat down cross-legged.
The Supreme Person sat down.
I beheld that Fully Enlightened One,
radiant and enchanting.
Like a blooming blue lotus,
like a blazing sacrificial fire,
like a burning lamp-tree.
Like lightning in the sky,
or like a fully blossomed king of sāl trees,
I beheld the Leader of the World.
This Naga, the Great Hero,
the Sage who brings an end to suffering—
having come into his presence, [one attains peace].
They are liberated from all suffering.
Having seen the God of Gods,
I observed his physical marks.
Is he truly enlightened or not?
Come, let me see him, the One with Vision.
His wheels possess a thousand spokes.
His supreme feet were visible;
having seen his marks,
I reached a definitive conclusion regarding the Tathāgata.
Having taken a broom and swept it clean at that time,
I then gathered flowers.
I worshipped the Best of Buddhas.
Having worshipped that Buddha,
who has crossed the flood and is free from taints;
Having arranged my deerskin garment over one shoulder,
I paid homage to the Leader of the World.
By means of that knowledge, the Perfectly Awakened One—
He dwells free from taints;
I shall proclaim that knowledge—
listen as I speak.
“Self-existent One of immeasurable glory, you have uplifted this world;
it is by coming into your presence that we have been saved.”
They cross over the stream of doubt.
You are the teacher and the banner,
the standard and the sacrificial post for living beings.
The ultimate refuge, the support,
the island, and the supreme among bipeds— it is possible to measure the water in the ocean, but not the virtues of the Buddha.
It might be possible to measure [the water] with a dry measure,
but it is not at all possible to measure your omniscient knowledge.
It is possible to hold the earth upon the surface of a scale, but not so,
O All-Knowing One, can [your merit] be measured.
Knowledge can indeed be maintained.
Space can be measured with a cord or even with a finger; [but knowledge cannot be measured].
But it is not possible to measure your omniscient knowledge;
it is like the water in the great ocean.
The earth, with its ridges and roots,
when compared to the wisdom of a Buddha,
does not serve as a fitting analogy.
Those whose minds operate within the world including its devas—
these are caught within the net.
O Visionary One, this is your knowledge.
By means of that knowledge, you have attained the complete and supreme enlightenment.
"By that knowledge you are omniscient;
you have crushed the followers of other sects.
Having recited these verses, he praised him.
A seer named Suruci,
having spread out his antelope skin,
sat down upon the ground.
Eighty-four thousand [yojanas] it plunges deep into the great ocean,
and it rises up just as high.
Neru is called the king of mountains;
it is so exceedingly lofty,
and it is long and broad as well.
Pulverized into minute fragments by the hundreds of thousands of millions,
even when being counted by the lakhs, [it was not exhausted].
It reached its end;
but your omniscient knowledge, O All-Knowing One, cannot be measured.
Whoever were to cast a fine-meshed net over the water,
whatever living beings there might be in the water—
They would be caught within the net.
Even so, O Great Hero,
whatever various sectarian teachers there may be;
Leaping into the thicket of views,
deluded by their grasping,
[they are overcome] by your pure knowledge.
"By you who see without obstruction,
these [beings] caught within the net do not surpass your knowledge."
At that time, the Blessed One,
the Greatly Renowned Anomadassi,
having emerged from meditative concentration, [sat upon his seat].
The Jina surveyed the direction.
Of the sage Anomadassi,
there was a disciple named Nisabha.
Surrounded by a hundred thousand who were taintless,
pure, of peaceful mind, and established in the state of a Tathāgata.
Having understood the mind of the Buddha, he approached the Leader of the World together with those possessing the six supernormal powers and skilled in meditation.
Standing there in the sky,
they circumambulated him to the right,
paying homage with palms joined.
He descended into the presence of the Buddha.
The Blessed One Anomadassī,
the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men;
Seated within the community of bhikkhus,
the Jina manifested coolness.
His attendant was named Varuṇa.
To the Teacher Anomadassi,
having arranged his robe over one shoulder,
he questioned the Leader of the World.
"What indeed, Blessed One,
is the cause for the Teacher’s smile?
For Buddhas do not smile without a reason."
They cause the white [robe] to be put on him.
The Blessed One Anomadassī,
the eldest in the world, the bull among men;
Sitting in the midst of the bhikkhus,
he spoke this verse:
“Whoever has honored me with a flower...”
And his knowledge was unsurpassed;
I shall proclaim that,
so listen as I speak.
Having understood the Buddha’s speech,
all the devas assembled,
desiring to hear the true Dhamma.
They approached the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In the ten world-systems,
the hosts of gods possessed of great psychic power;
Desiring to hear the true Dhamma,
they approached the Fully Awakened One.
“Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry— ”
And a fourfold army shall constantly attend upon him;
this is the fruit of making offerings to the Buddha.
Sixty thousand musical instruments and well-adorned drums shall constantly attend upon me.
This is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha:
sixteen thousand women,
beautifully adorned.
Adorned with various garments and ornaments,
wearing jeweled earrings,
with long eyelashes and smiling faces.
With beautiful consciousness and slender waists,
they shall constantly attend upon him;
this is the fruit of making offerings to the Buddha.
For a hundred thousand eons he will delight in the world of the gods;
a thousand times he will be a wheel-turning monarch.
He will be a king over the realm.
A thousand times, he will exercise divine sovereignty as a lord of the gods.
A vast regional sovereignty,
beyond counting,
was attained in his final existence.
He will go to the human state;
a brahmin woman named Sāriyā will carry him in her womb.
This man shall be known by his mother’s name and clan;
he shall be known by the name Sāriputta.
He will possess sharp wisdom.
Having abandoned eighty crores [of wealth],
he will go forth as one who owns nothing.
Seeking the state of peace,
he will wander this earth.
In immeasurable eons from now,
Born of the Okkāka clan,
he will be a teacher in the world named Gotama by lineage.
His heir in the Dhamma,
his own son, fashioned from the Dhamma—
Sāriputta by name.
He will become a chief disciple.
This Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā has its source in the Himavat mountains.
Just as rivers flow into the great ocean, filling that vast sea,
even so is this Sāriputta.
Confident in the three [knowledges],
having reached perfection in wisdom,
he will satisfy all living beings.
From the Himalayas up to the great ocean, the vast sea—
whatever sandy shore lies between them,
Though it is incalculable by number,
it can nevertheless be reckoned without remainder,
just as with any calculation.
But for Sāriputta, it will not be so;
he will perceive it even when the target is placed at a distance of a hundred thousand leagues.
The sands of the Ganges might come to an end,
but the measure of Sāriputta’s wisdom will never be reached.
In the great ocean, the waves are beyond counting;
even so it is with Sāriputta.
He will not exist as one who perceives [them].
Having propitiated the Fully Awakened One,
Gotama, the bull of the Sakyas;
Having reached perfection in wisdom,
he will become the foremost disciple when the Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion.
The Son of the Sakyan, who is such as he is,
will rightly follow [the path],
raining down showers of Dhamma.
Having directly known all this,
Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans,
sat down amidst the community of bhikkhus.
‘He will place me in the foremost position.
“O, how well done is my deed for the Teacher Anomadassi!
Having performed service for him,
I reached perfection in every respect;
immeasurable was the karma I performed.
It showed me its fruit right here;
like an arrow released from a bow,
I have utterly consumed my defilements.
Seeking the unconditioned,
the unshakable state of Nibbāna,
he scrutinized all the various sectarians.
Thus have I wandered through existence,
just as a sick man would search for medicine.
One who is afflicted with disease should seek out the entire forest,
searching for the unconditioned.
Nirvana is the deathless state;
five hundred unbroken [disciples] went forth into the ascetic life of a seer.
Burdened by a mass of matted hair,
clothed in an upper garment of antelope skin,
having reached the perfection of direct knowledge—
I went to the Brahma-world.
There is no purity among outsiders,
except for the teaching of the Conqueror.
Whatever beings possess intelligence,
they are purified in the teaching of the Conqueror;
this is based on personal effort.
"This is not mere hearsay";
seeking the unconditioned,
I wandered through false fords.
Just as a person seeking heartwood might cut down a plantain tree and split it open,
yet find no heartwood therein;
For it is empty of essence;
likewise, the many people among the world's sectarians hold various views.
You are empty of the unconditioned,
like a plantain tree of its core;
now that you have reached your final existence, [you are empty].
I was once a mere kinsman of Brahmins;
having renounced great wealth,
I went forth into the homeless life.
The First Recitation Section.
“A reciter, a bearer of the mantras,
one who has mastered the three Vedas;”
There is a brahmin named Sañcaya;
I dwell at his feet as your disciple, O Great Hero.
A brahmin named Assaji,
difficult to approach and of fierce energy,
was then wandering for alms.
I saw that wise sage, absorbed in silence,
his mind at peace, a great elephant.
Just like a fully blossomed lotus,
upon seeing him— well-tamed and pure in mind— a thought arose within me.
This bull-like, excellent hero will become an Arhat;
he moves with a graceful deportment.
Handsome and well-restrained,
tamed in the highest taming,
he will become a seer of the Deathless.
What if I were now to ask about the supreme goal him whose mind is satisfied?
Being questioned by me, he will explain it to me.
I then asked him a question.
As he was walking for alms,
I followed behind him.
Seeking an opportunity to ask about the deathless state,
he approached one who had arrived in the middle of the street.
Having approached, I asked:
"How is your lineage, O Hero?
Whose disciple are you, dear sir?"
Thus questioned by me,
he replied like an unafraid lion:
"A Buddha has arisen in the world."
“I am his disciple, friend.
“Of what sort is he, O Great Hero,
you who have followed him, O one of great renown?”
"O sir, please tell me well the Dhamma, the teaching of the Buddha.
Thus questioned by me, he explained everything to me.
The profound and subtle state,
the slayer of the arrow of craving,
the dispeller of all suffering.
“Of those phenomena that arise from a cause,
the Tathāgata has stated their cause,
as well as their cessation.”
“Such is the teaching of the Great Recluse.
When this question was answered,
I attained the first fruit.
I became stainless and pure after hearing the teaching of the Victor;
having heard the word of the Sage, I became free from passion.
Having seen the supreme Dhamma and having fully penetrated the true Dhamma,
I spoke this verse.
“If you were to realize that very Dhamma right now,
you would attain the sorrowless state,
unseen and passed beyond.”
"Through many hundreds of thousands of eons,
while seeking the Dhamma,
I wandered through difficult fords."
Thus my purpose has been attained;
it is time for me not to be negligent.
I am satisfied with Assaji.
Having attained the unshakable state,
I went to the hermitage seeking a companion.
Seeing me from afar,
my well-trained companion,
perfected in the modes of conduct, approached.
He spoke these words:
“Your face and eyes are serene;
the very nature of a sage is visible.”
I hope you have attained the deathless,
the state of Nibbāna, the imperishable;
you have come here in a manner befitting your beauty.
Like one who has performed the imperturbable deed;
like an elephant tamed by training,
you are stilled, O Brahmin.
“I have attained the Deathless,
which removes the dart of sorrow;
you too shall attain it.”
"Let us go into the presence of the Buddha.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," my well-trained companion [responded].
Taking each other by the hand,
having approached your presence,
we both shall go forth.
In the presence of the Son of the Sakyas;
having come to your teaching,
we dwell free from taints.
Kolita is supreme in psychic power,
and I have reached the further shore in wisdom; both of us,
having come together as one, [will go forth].
We shall adorn the Teaching.
With my purpose still unfulfilled,
I wandered at a false ford.
Having come into your presence,
my aspiration has been fulfilled.
Having established myself upon the earth, I stand firm.
In season the trees blossom;
they emit divine fragrances and gladden all living beings.
In the same way, O Great Hero,
Son of the Sakyas of great renown,
having established myself in your teaching, I shall remain steadfast.
I shall cause it to blossom.
Seeking the flower of liberation that releases one from the cycle of existence, I shall strive.
By means of obtaining the flower of liberation,
I satisfy all living beings throughout the entire extent of the Buddha-field.
Setting aside the Great Sage,
there is no one equal to your son in wisdom, O Visionary One.
Your disciples are well-trained,
and your assembly is well-disciplined;
they have been tamed by the highest training.
The wise ones, meditative and delighting in jhāna, with peaceful minds and concentrated, always attend upon him.
Sages endowed with the perfection of wisdom always surround you—
those who have few desires, who are prudent, and wise.
Eating little and free from greed,
content with both gain and loss,
they always attend upon him.
Forest-dwellers, delighting in ascetic practices,
meditators wearing coarse robes,
the wise who rejoice in seclusion.
They always surround him:
those practicing the path and those established in the fruit,
those in training and those possessing the fruits.
Those who aspire to the supreme goal always surround him;
so too do the stainless stream-enterers.
The once-returners and those who do not return, as well as the arahants,
always surround him.
Skilled in the foundations of mindfulness and delighting in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment—
many such disciples you have, all of them.
They always attend upon him—
those skilled in the bases of psychic power,
who delight in the cultivation of concentration.
Those devoted to the right efforts always surround him;
they possess the three knowledges and the six super-knowledges.
Having reached perfection in supernormal power and having attained perfection in wisdom,
they always attend upon you.
Such are your disciples, O Great Hero,
well-trained by you;
difficult to approach and of fierce power.
They always attend upon him.
Surrounded by those disciplined ascetic disciples, he—
Fearless like the king of beasts,
you shine like the lord of the stars;
having established yourself upon the earth, you stand firm.
The trees grow upon the earth;
they reach full maturity and display their fruit.
You are like the earth,
O Son of the Sakyas, of great renown;
having established yourself in your teaching—
They obtain the fruit of immortality.
The rivers Sindhu, Sarassatī, and Candabhāgā;
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā,
the Sarabhū and the Mahī—
of these as they flow along,
Sāgara accepted;
they abandoned their former name and were known as Sāgarottha alone.
In the same way, these four castes,
having gone forth into homelessness in your presence,
abandon their former names.
They are known as the sons of the Buddha.
Just as the stainless moon moves through the expanse of space;
He outshines all the hosts of stars in the world with his radiance;
even so do you, O Great Hero.
Surrounded by gods and humans;
having surpassed all these,
you shine forever.
The waves that arise in the deep do not overstep the shore;
they all reach the very shore.
Just as those [grains], being crushed, scatter about,
so too do the many people of various views among the world’s sectarians.
Desiring to proclaim the Dhamma,
they do not overstep that Sage;
and if they reach him, [they find no fault].
O Eyeful One, oppose them!
Upon reaching Tavantika,
they will be utterly crushed to pieces.
Just as many water-born lilies and lotuses, though born in the water,
are not defiled by the water, so too...
And with the mire of mud.
In the same way, many beings born in the world grow in discord.
Afflicted by passion and hatred,
like a white lotus in the mud;
just as a water-born lotus, [remains unstained].
It grows in the midst of the water,
yet it is not smeared by the water,
for the lotus is pure.
In just that way, O Great Hero,
you who were born into the world as a Great Sage,
are not defiled by the world.
Just as a lotus [is born] from water,
and just as many water-born flowers bloom in the month of Ramma.
They do not bypass that month;
it is the season for their blossoming.
Even so, O Great Hero, you—
You have blossomed through liberation;
they do not overstep your teaching,
just as the water-born lotus is not submerged by the water.
The king of sāl trees is in full bloom,
wafting a divine fragrance;
it stands surrounded by other sāl trees.
Like the king of sāl trees, you shine;
even so, O Great Hero,
you are in full bloom with the wisdom of a Buddha.
Surrounded by the community of bhikkhus,
you shine like a king of sal trees;
just as Mount Himavat, the mountain of snow.
It is the medicine for all living beings;
it is the abode of the nāgas, the asuras, and the deities.
In the same way, O Great Hero,
you are like a medicine for living beings,
possessing the three knowledges and the six direct insights.
They have reached perfection in supernormal power.
Having been instructed by you, O Great Hero,
those compassionate ones—
They delight in the joy of the Dhamma and dwell in your teaching,
like Sīha, the king of beasts.
Having gone forth from its dwelling,
it surveys the four quarters and roars three times.
All deer tremble with fear when the king of beasts roars;
for he is truly one of noble birth.
He constantly terrifies the beasts.
O Great Hero, as you roar,
the earth trembles all around.
Those who are to be awakened awaken;
the hosts of Māra tremble.
All the heretics tremble.
As you roar, O Great Sage,
the crows have fled from the army like deer from the king of beasts.
Whatever teachers there may be in the world who are called "leaders of a group," [they have all] received the Dhamma handed down through succession.
They teach the Dhamma to the assembly;
but you, O Great Hero,
do not teach the Dhamma to living beings in such a manner.
Having awakened to the truths by oneself,
having fully realized the factors conducive to enlightenment, and having known one's own latent tendencies and underlying inclinations,
Having discerned the strength and weakness of the faculties,
and who is capable and who is incapable,
you thunder like a great cloud.
Even if an assembly were seated as far as the limits of the world-system,
investigating various views—
To cut through their doubt,
the Sage, skilled in similes, having understood the minds of all, [spoke this].
While explaining even a single question,
you cut away the doubts of living beings—
just as you did for one like Upatissa.
Even if the entire earth were filled with them,
all those people with palms joined in reverence would praise the Leader of the World.
Even if they were to praise you for an eon, praising you in various ways,
they would not be able to measure [your qualities].
The Tathāgata is immeasurable;
for the Conqueror has been praised by me according to my own power.
Even if they were to praise it for ten million eons,
they would praise it in this very way. For if some deity or...
Even a well-trained man,
if he were to attempt to deceive [the Buddha],
would only meet with frustration.
Having established yourself in the Teaching,
O Greatly Famed Son of the Sakyas,
you have reached the perfection of wisdom.
I dwell free from taints;
I crush the followers of other sects and I maintain the teaching of the Conqueror.
Today, O General of the Dhamma,
in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans,
you have performed a deed of immeasurable merit.
It bore fruit for me right here;
like an arrow discharged by Sukhittha,
it incinerated my defilements.
Whatever person should always carry a burden upon their head,
they would be distressed by that burden.
So too, burdened by burdens,
I wandered through various states of existence, burning with the three fires.
Burdened by the weight of existence,
like a mountain that has been climbed;
now the burden has been laid down by me.
The states of existence have been demolished by me;
everything that was to be done has been accomplished in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyas.
To the extent that there is within the Buddha-field,
excluding the Bull of the Sakyas,
I am foremost in wisdom.
My equal is not to be found.
I am highly skilled in meditative concentration and have reached the perfection of supernormal powers.
If I so desired, today I could manifest a thousand [forms].
Of this successive dwelling, [I am the master].
The Great Sage, having attained mastery,
taught the Dispensation to me:
"Cessation is my bed."
My divine eye is purified,
I am skilled in concentration,
and I am devoted to the right efforts.
Delighting in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment,
I have indeed accomplished everything that is to be attained by a disciple.
Except for Lokanātha,
there is no one equal to me;
I am skilled in the meditative attainments.
I am one who quickly attains the jhānas and liberations;
delighting in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment,
I have reached the perfection of the qualities of a disciple.
Even by the disciple’s virtue of Phussa,
the bearer of the burden was liberated through wisdom;
that mind which is embraced by faith—
Always [be humble] toward fellow practitioners of the holy life—
like a snake whose venom has been removed,
like a bull with its horns broken.
Having cast aside pride and conceit,
I approach the assembly with profound reverence.
If she were possessed of form, [I would honor her].
Even the earth with all its wealth would not equal my wisdom;
this is the fruit of the veneration of knowledge for the Blessed One Anomadassi.
The Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the Sakyan son, the Tādi;
may I follow it rightly.
This is the fruit of the praise of knowledge.
May I never be one of evil desires,
nor ever be lazy or of inferior energy.
One who has heard little and is ill-behaved may at times be well-regarded;
but one who is learned and wise—
Well-composed in the precepts and devoted to mental tranquility,
let him stand even upon the summit of a mountain.
I say this to you, O venerable ones,
as many as are gathered here:
be of few desires and be content.
A meditator always delighting in jhāna,
having seen me first,
became stainless and pure.
Thus my teacher was the wise one named Assaji, my disciple;
by his guidance, today—
I was the General of the Dhamma;
having reached perfection in all things,
I dwell free from taints.
The one who was my teacher,
the disciple named Assaji—
whichever direction he dwells in, [there I go].
I placed it upon my head.
Recalling my deed, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyas, [acted accordingly].
Having sat within the community of bhikkhus,
he placed me in the foremost position.
My defilements have been incinerated.
All states of existence have been utterly eradicated;
like a snake that has severed its bonds,
I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me in the presence of the Best of Buddhas;
the three true knowledges have been attained.
This is the teaching of the Buddha:
the four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations.
"The six direct knowledges have been realized;
the Buddha's teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed did the Elder Venerable Sāriputta speak these verses.
The legend of the Elder Sāriputta is first.
